transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-01-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jonas Patel (Redwood SE), Rita Alvarez (Apollo CTO), Marcus Lin (Lead Backend), Sophie O'Neil (MLOps), Cedric Park (Product)

Summary (auto): quick hosted api demo covering streaming, params, and retry patterns; security and pilot follow-ups.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood inference, joining me is jonas se who will do the demo - hey jonas
[00:08] Jonas Patel: hey all, thanks for making time. quick agenda, we'll run through hosted chat endpoint, streaming behavior, param knobs (temp, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences), retry/backoff patterns and then a short Console peek and Optimize suggestion set.
[00:22] Rita Alvarez: sounds good, we're mostly concerned about latency for our live tracking UI and also data residency. we'll chime in as we go.
[00:30] Marcus Lin: also want to understand cost impact when we change batching or tokenization — we do real-time updates every 2s for location feed so latency matters.
[00:38] Jonas Patel: good context. quickly, hosted api supports streaming responses so you can start rendering partial tokens immediately. default streamer is chunked deltas, and we have configurable "stream_chunk_ms" behavior, ah that's internal name but you'll see the param in the SDK/console.
[00:52] Jonas Patel: demo start — console -> APIs -> Chat -> create new call. i'm sending a prompt: "Summarize latest telemetry: vehicle 412 is 3 minutes behind schedule". hitting run with streaming on.
[01:10] [Demo audio: keyboard clicks]
[01:15] Jonas Patel: you can see partial tokens come over via server-sent events, on the client side we buffer until punctuation or newline depending on your render strategy. important to know streaming doesn't change billing semantics — tokens are billed as generated.
[01:30] Cedric Park: is it possible to get the first token latency down to sub-150ms? our current infra target is 200ms p95 for initial token.
[01:39] Jonas Patel: sub-150ms is aggressive on shared hosted plans for cold prompts, we typically see 120-300ms first-token in best-case with our smallest models but for guaranteed p95 you'd look at Dedicated or pinned instances. for hosted you can tune with smaller model family or warm prefixes and kv cache.
[01:55] Marcus Lin: can you explain kv cache briefly? we heard about it in your docs but not sure how it helps live chat.
[02:03] Jonas Patel: sure — kv cache persists key/value tensors for prior tokens on the GPU so repeats or long conversations don't re-compute attention. for streaming it's helpful because if you have many turns with the same system prompt you can avoid re-encoding that each time — saves latency and cost. in hosted we manage cache automatically when you set conversation_id or session_id in the request.
[02:25] Rita Alvarez: is conversation_id persisted across regions? we have users in eu and na and need data residency.
[02:32] Maya Chen: good question — hosted store is regioned, we have EU and NA regions; conversation metadata and KV remain in region. for strict residency and audit controls you'd want Private deployment with a VPC or on-prem box.
[02:46] Sophie O'Neil: do you support customer-managed KMS? encryption at rest is a requirement for us.
[02:52] Maya Chen: yes, we integrate with customer KMS for Private and Dedicated; hosted has server-side managed keys but we can discuss a managed key option in enterprise plan — i'll follow up with details and KMS whitepaper.
[03:05] Jonas Patel: back to params — temperature controls sampling randomness; top_p is nucleus sampling. lower temperature and top_p make model more deterministic which helps reproducibility of safety triggers. max_tokens and stop sequences are how you bound generation. also talk about idempotency key for retries.
[03:27] Marcus Lin: what's the recommended retry strategy for ephemeral network errors? we see 503s occasionally in other vendors.
[03:33] Jonas Patel: recommended pattern: short exponential backoff with jitter, keep low max attempts (2-3) for UI flows so you don't double charge or cause duplicated side-effects. use idempotency_key to safely retry server operations. also for streaming if you lose connection we return a resume cursor for compatible clients — though resume is model-dependent.
[03:55] Rita Alvarez: you mentioned cost vs latency tradeoffs. any concrete numbers?
[04:00] Jonas Patel: rough ballpark: using a smaller quantized model reduces token cost by ~3-4x and median latency by ~20-40%, but quality may degrade on complex prompts. batching (concurrency) helps throughput but increases tail latency for single interactive requests unless you configure dynamic batching thresholds. our Console's Optimize tab will give suggestions based on your token distribution.
[04:25] Jonas Patel: opening the Console -> Optimize -> Recommendations. you can upload sample payloads or connect usage logs; we run analysis and suggest batching sizes, quantization profiles (int8 vs int4 tradeoffs) and caching opportunities.
[04:40] Sophie O'Neil: can we try a small pilot to measure p95 with our actual payloads?
[04:44] Maya Chen: yes, that's what most teams do. we can run a 2-week pilot with limited QPS. jonas will prepare a benchmark script and runbook.
[04:54] Jonas Patel: i'll need a sample set: typical prompt length, avg tokens in responses, and concurrency targets. marcus, that would come from you.
[05:02] Marcus Lin: i'll export a week's traffic and share distribution — are there any sample schema you prefer?
[05:07] Jonas Patel: CSV with columns: prompt_text, response_tokens_estimate, timestamp, and route name is fine. i'll provide a template.
[05:14] [00:05:15] Cedric Park: curious about fallback patterns — if hosted can't meet latency, do you automatically fallback to smaller model?
[05:22] Jonas Patel: yes, we have smart routing and fallback policies. you can configure a policy by latency or cost threshold — if p95 exceeds limit, traffic can route to a cheaper quantized variant or to another region. automatic fallback preserves responses but may affect quality.
[05:38] Rita Alvarez: what about observability and tracing? we need per-token cost and per-request traces tied to our request ids.
[05:45] Maya Chen: Console provides per-route token breakdown, latency histograms, and a tracing hook where you can send request-id; logs are retained per your plan, and audit logs are available for enterprise.
[05:56] Marcus Lin: are audit logs tamper-evident? we have compliance with logistics regs.
[06:01] Maya Chen: audit logs use append-only storage and we can integrate with your SIEM and a write-once store for retention. we'll include the compliance whitepaper.
[06:10] Jonas Patel: quick note on retries for streaming — if the client disconnects mid-stream we recommend resuming on resume_token if available, otherwise issue a idempotent retry that replays the prompt and uses the same idempotency key so the model can regenerate deterministically; this depends on temperature and state — lower temp helps deterministic replay.
[06:34] [06:34] Marcus Lin: how do you charge for partial streams if client disconnects halfway?
[06:38] Maya Chen: billing is per token generated. if the server already generated tokens before the disconnect those are billed. we can mitigate cost by lowering max_tokens and controlling early stop sequences in UI flows.
[06:50] Cedric Park: any limits on concurrent streams per account?
[06:54] Maya Chen: hosted has practical per-account concurrency defaults; you can request increases. for tight SLOs Dedicated reserved capacity is better since you get predictable throughput.
[07:05] [07:05] Jonas Patel: demo switch — code snippet. here's a node snippet showing streaming via EventSource and reconnect logic with exponential backoff and jitter. //snippet
[07:20] Jonas Patel: note the idempotency header we set: X-Idempotency-Key: <uuid>. also we set conversation_id for kv cache.
[07:30] Sophie O'Neil: will conversation_id create privacy concerns? we store user identifiers?
[07:34] Maya Chen: we recommend hashing or using internal session ids; the platform doesn't require PII in the prompt. conversation metadata can be stored as opaque ids to meet privacy needs.
[07:46] [07:46] Marcus Lin: what about rate limiting — do you return a Retry-After header?
[07:50] Jonas Patel: yes, standard 429 responses include Retry-After and a body with quota details. console also shows quota windows. you can configure burst policies for Dedicated.
[08:01] Rita Alvarez: we'd like to see an example of a failover where the region is degraded and traffic goes to fallback region — can you simulate during pilot?
[08:10] Maya Chen: we can demo a simulated failover and show rollbacks and A/B routing in the console during the pilot kickoff.
[08:18] [08:18] Jonas Patel: a couple pitfalls folks hit — using too-high temperature for deterministic tasks, forgetting idempotency for interactive side-effecting calls, and not bounding max_tokens for UI flows which leads to cost surprises.
[08:34] Cedric Park: Competitors we're weighing in: OtherCloudAI has slightly cheaper token rates but slower streaming; Self-hosted Forge gives more control but higher ops cost.
[08:44] Maya Chen: that's the tradeoff. Redwood focuses on predictable serving with tooling to optimize costs.
[08:50] [08:50] Jonas Patel: quick Console tour: route config -> retries -> fallback policies -> per-route Optimize suggestions. i'm toggling a canary rollout to 10% and setting fallback to a quantized small model.
[09:05] Sophie O'Neil: will canary metrics automatically compare quality regressions?
[09:09] Jonas Patel: yes, the rollout page can run A/B comparisons on latency, cost, and a custom eval set you upload — we can wire your QA prompts to check for regressions.
[09:22] Rita Alvarez: what's the SLA on hosted? we prefer 99.9 for production.
[09:27] Maya Chen: hosted SLA varies by plan; Dedicated has the stronger 99.9 uptime guarantee with latency targets you can negotiate on reserved capacity. we'll include SLA options in the follow-up.
[09:38] Marcus Lin: ok, can we summarize next steps?
[09:41] Maya Chen: yes — action items: maya sends SOC2 + KMS note, jonas prepares benchmark script + runbook, marcus share sample payloads. schedule pilot kickoff.
[09:52] Rita Alvarez: sounds good. also please include sample client reconnect pattern we can embed.
[09:57] Maya Chen: will do. any other questions?
[10:00] Cedric Park: none from me. thanks.
[10:03] Maya Chen: great — thanks everyone for the time. we'll follow up with the docs and bench script.

End of transcript.
